# Course Structure {.unnumbered}

This book collects the course materials for PHC 506. Here's how it's organized
and how to get the most out of it.

## The lectures build on each other

The material is split into four lectures (see the sidebar for the full list):

1. **R Fundamentals**---R and RStudio, the basics of the language, functions,
   lists, and data frames.
2. **Working with Data Frames**---manipulating tabular data, calculations by
   row or group, and handling dates, factors, and missing values.
3. **Plotting**---base graphics and building up visualizations with ggplot2.
4. **Programming**---writing functions, flow control, loops, scoping, and
   combining and reshaping data.

Everything is **cumulative**: each lecture assumes the ones before it, so it's
worth working through them in order and not skipping ahead. We cover this
material interactively during class, but you can also read and work through it
beforehand.

## How each lecture works

A lecture isn't just something to read---it's something to *do*. Each one mixes
three kinds of content:

- **Notes and worked examples** that explain a concept, with runnable code and
  its output shown inline.
- **Fill-in examples**---deliberately incomplete snippets for you to complete.
  Typing code yourself (rather than only reading it) is a big part of learning to
  program, so don't skip these.
- **Breakout problems**---short exercises you solve on your own, and then we
  work through together in class.

## Running the code

You can work through the material two ways:

- **Locally in RStudio.** Use the **download button** in the sidebar to grab a
  zip of the lecture files and project, then open it in RStudio. See
  [Installing R and RStudio](installing_r_rstudio.qmd) to get set up.
- **In your browser.** The breakout exercises are interactive: edit the code and
  press *Run* to execute it, with no installation required. The first time you
  run a cell it takes a moment to start up R, then it's quick.

The interactive cells are the fastest way to experiment, but doing the work in
RStudio is closest to how you'll use R in practice.

## Tips for success

- **Try the exercises on your own first.** Course assessments will look similar,
  so the practice matters.
- **Don't fear the red text.** Errors are normal---experts hit them constantly.
  Read the message, adjust, and try again.
- **There's usually more than one right answer.** If your code works and you can
  read it later, that's a good solution.
- **Programming is a new way of thinking.** It's a language, and like any
  language it gets easier with practice. Stick with it.
